summary.text: Any admissible sequence of length at least three ends in either \(1\) or \(2\); in the latter case its penultimate entry must be \(1\). Splitting further according as the preceding prefix already contains \(1\) (respectively \(2\)), deletion followed by subtracting \(0\) or \(1\) (respectively \(1\) or \(2\)) gives four disjoint reversible classes, hence the recurrence \(b_N=2b_{N-1}+2b_{N-2}\); the direct initial counts \(b_1=1\) and \(b_2=3\) complete the identification.

full_proof.text:
Let a sequence of length \(L\) mean a tuple
\[
 x=(x_1,\ldots,x_L)
\]
of positive integers. Call such a tuple good if it has the following two properties.

1. If \(M=\max_i x_i\), then every integer in \(\{1,2,\ldots,M\}\) occurs among the entries of \(x\). Thus the set of values occurring in \(x\) covers an initial interval of the positive integers.
2. Whenever \(i<j\) and \(j\ne i+1\), one has \(x_i\ge x_j\). Equivalently, whenever two entries occur in increasing positions but are not adjacent, the earlier entry is at least the later one.

Write \(\mathcal G_L\) for the set of good sequences of length \(L\), and write \(b_L=|\mathcal G_L|\). We shall prove that
\[
 b_1=1,\qquad b_2=3,
\]
and, for every \(L\ge 1\),
\[
 b_{L+2}=2b_{L+1}+2b_L. \tag{1}
\]
This will establish that \(b_{n+1}=a(n)\), where \(a(0)=1\), \(a(1)=3\), and
\[
 a(n+2)=2a(n+1)+2a(n).
\]
We will then also identify this recurrence with the usual enumeration of ternary strings avoiding consecutive zeros.

First observe a basic consequence of the covering condition: every good sequence contains an entry equal to \(1\). Indeed, its maximum is at least \(1\), since all entries are positive, and hence the covering condition requires \(1\) to occur.

We next establish two structural facts about the end of a good sequence of length at least three. Let
\[
 y=(y_1,\ldots,y_{L+2})\in\mathcal G_{L+2},
\]
where \(L\ge1\).

We claim first that
\[
 y_{L+2}\in\{1,2\}. \tag{2}
\]
Suppose instead that \(y_{L+2}\ge3\). Because the sequence covers all values up to its maximum, both \(1\) and \(2\) occur somewhere in the sequence. Neither can occur in the final position, whose value is at least \(3\). Moreover, an occurrence of either \(1\) or \(2\) cannot be earlier than the penultimate position: if \(i\le L\), then positions \(i\) and \(L+2\) are non-adjacent, so the order condition would give
\[
 y_i\ge y_{L+2}\ge3,
\]
contrary to \(y_i\in\{1,2\}\). Therefore every occurrence of both \(1\) and \(2\) would have to be in the single penultimate position \(L+1\), which is impossible. This proves (2).

The second structural fact is that if
\[
 y_{L+2}=2,
\]
then necessarily
\[
 y_{L+1}=1. \tag{3}
\]
The covering condition requires an occurrence of \(1\). It is not in the last position. If it occurred at a position \(i\le L\), then that position would be non-adjacent to the last position, and the order condition would imply \(1=y_i\ge y_{L+2}=2\), a contradiction. Hence the required \(1\) occurs in the penultimate position, proving (3).

We now give a complete classification of \(\mathcal G_{L+2}\) into four disjoint families. For a tuple \(x\), let \(x+q\) denote the tuple obtained by adding \(q\) to each of its entries. Define four constructions:
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(x)&=(x,1) &&(x\in\mathcal G_{L+1}),\\
B(x)&=(x+1,1) &&(x\in\mathcal G_{L+1}),\\
C(x)&=(x+1,1,2) &&(x\in\mathcal G_L),\\
D(x)&=(x+2,1,2) &&(x\in\mathcal G_L).
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
Here commas indicate concatenation.

We first check that all four constructions produce good sequences.

For \(A(x)=(x,1)\), positivity is immediate. Since a good nonempty tuple \(x\) already contains \(1\), appending another \(1\) does not change its maximum or the set of values needed for initial-interval coverage. The order condition among positions in the old prefix is inherited from \(x\). Any old position that is non-adjacent to the new last position has a positive value and therefore has value at least \(1\), as required.

For \(B(x)=(x+1,1)\), suppose the maximum of \(x\) is \(M\). The shifted prefix contains every value from \(2\) through \(M+1\), and the appended final entry supplies \(1\). Thus the new sequence covers \(1,\ldots,M+1\), which is exactly the interval up to its new maximum. Adding the same constant to all old entries preserves all order comparisons among them, and every shifted old entry is at least \(2\), hence at least the appended \(1\).

For \(C(x)=(x+1,1,2)\), if the maximum of \(x\) is \(M\), then \(M\ge1\), and the shifted prefix contains \(2,3,\ldots,M+1\). The penultimate entry supplies \(1\), while the final \(2\) is already among the covered values. Hence the new maximum is \(M+1\), and all values from \(1\) to \(M+1\) occur. Comparisons within the shifted prefix are inherited from \(x\). Every shifted prefix entry is at least \(2\), so it is at least both the penultimate value \(1\) and, whenever the positions are non-adjacent, the final value \(2\). The final two positions are adjacent, so no comparison between \(1\) and \(2\) is required.

For \(D(x)=(x+2,1,2)\), the shifted prefix contains \(3,4,\ldots,M+2\), and the two appended entries supply \(1\) and \(2\). Thus every value through the new maximum \(M+2\) occurs. Order within the prefix is preserved by the common shift, and each shifted prefix entry is at least \(3\), so all required comparisons with the appended \(1\) and \(2\) hold.

It remains to show that every good sequence belongs to exactly one of these four families. Let
\[
 y=(y_1,\ldots,y_{L+2})\in\mathcal G_{L+2}.
\]
By (2), its final entry is either \(1\) or \(2\).

Case 1: \(y_{L+2}=1\).

Consider the prefix
\[
 p=(y_1,\ldots,y_{L+1}).
\]
There are two subcases.

If \(p\) contains a \(1\), then \(p\) itself is good. Positivity and the order condition are inherited from \(y\). For coverage, take any value required up to the maximum of \(p\). It occurs somewhere in \(y\). If its occurrence is in the prefix, there is nothing to prove. The only possible obstruction is that the chosen occurrence is the deleted last entry, but that entry has value \(1\), and by assumption another \(1\) occurs in the prefix. Thus every required value occurs in \(p\). Consequently
\[
 y=A(p).
\]

If \(p\) contains no \(1\), then every entry of \(p\) is at least \(2\). Define
\[
 x=(y_1-1,\ldots,y_{L+1}-1).
\]
This is a positive tuple. Subtracting the same constant from every entry preserves all required weak inequalities. It also preserves initial-interval coverage after shifting the interval down by one: if the maximum of \(p\) is \(M\), then the maximum of \(x\) is \(M-1\). For each \(k\in\{1,\ldots,M-1\}\), the value \(k+1\) lies between \(2\) and \(M\), so it occurs in \(y\) by coverage. It cannot occur at the last position, whose value is \(1\); hence it occurs in \(p\), and therefore \(k\) occurs in \(x\). Thus \(x\in\mathcal G_{L+1}\), and
\[
 y=B(x).
\]
This completes the last-entry-\(1\) case.

Case 2: \(y_{L+2}=2\).

By (3), \(y_{L+1}=1\). Let the earlier prefix be
\[
 p=(y_1,\ldots,y_L).
\]
Every entry of \(p\) is at least \(2\): each such position is non-adjacent to the final position, so the order condition gives \(y_i\ge y_{L+2}=2\).

Again there are two subcases. Suppose first that \(p\) contains a \(2\). Define
\[
 x=(y_1-1,\ldots,y_L-1).
\]
The entries of \(x\) are positive, and all required inequalities are inherited after subtracting \(1\). We verify coverage. The occurrence of \(2\) in \(p\) supplies an occurrence of \(1\) in \(x\). For any larger required value \(k\) of \(x\), the value \(k+1\ge3\) is required in \(y\). It cannot be either of the last two entries, whose values are \(1\) and \(2\), so it occurs in \(p\), giving an occurrence of \(k\) in \(x\). Equivalently, if the maximum of \(p\) is \(M\), then \(x\) covers every value from \(1\) through \(M-1\). Hence \(x\in\mathcal G_L\), and
\[
 y=C(x)=(x+1,1,2).
\]

Finally, suppose that \(p\) contains no \(2\). Since every entry of \(p\) is at least \(2\), it is then in fact at least \(3\). Define
\[
 x=(y_1-2,\ldots,y_L-2).
\]
This is positive and inherits the order condition. If the maximum of \(p\) is \(M\), then for every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,M-2\}\), the value \(k+2\), which is at least \(3\), must occur in \(y\). It cannot occur in either of the final two positions, so it occurs in \(p\), and therefore \(k\) occurs in \(x\). Thus \(x\) covers the initial interval through its maximum \(M-2\), so \(x\in\mathcal G_L\), and
\[
 y=D(x)=(x+2,1,2).
\]

This proves that the four constructions in (4) are exhaustive. They are also disjoint and injective. Injectivity of each construction is immediate: delete the appended entries and subtract the indicated constant to recover the original tuple. The images of \(A\) and \(B\) have final entry \(1\), while those of \(C\) and \(D\) have final entry \(2\), so the first pair is disjoint from the second pair.

To see that the images of \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, suppose
\[
 A(x)=B(z)

after construction from good tuples \(x,z\in\mathcal G_{L+1}\). The good tuple \(x\) contains an entry equal to \(1\). At the corresponding position, equality of the constructed prefixes would say
\[
 1=z_i+1,
\]
so \(z_i=0\), contradicting positivity. Similarly, if \(C(x)=D(z)\) for good \(x,z\in\mathcal G_L\), choose a position where \(x_i=1\). Equality there would give
\[
 x_i+1=z_i+2,
\]
so again \(z_i=0\), a contradiction. Thus all four families are pairwise disjoint.

We have therefore established the disjoint decomposition
\[
\mathcal G_{L+2}
 =A(\mathcal G_{L+1})\,\dot\cup\,
 B(\mathcal G_{L+1})\,\dot\cup\,
 C(\mathcal G_L)\,\dot\cup\,
 D(\mathcal G_L)
\]
for every \(L\ge1\). In particular, this decomposition inductively shows that all the sets involved are finite, and taking cardinalities gives
\[
 b_{L+2}=b_{L+1}+b_{L+1}+b_L+b_L
 =2b_{L+1}+2b_L,
\]
which is (1).

It remains to determine the initial values. A good sequence of length one must be \((1)\). Indeed, if its sole entry were larger than \(1\), the covering condition would require \(1\) also to occur, which is impossible. Hence
\[
 b_1=1.
\]

For length two, the order condition imposes nothing because the two positions are adjacent. The covering condition and positivity leave exactly
\[
 (1,1),\qquad (2,1),\qquad (1,2).
\]
To justify that there are no others, the last-entry argument (2), which also applies to length two, says the last entry is \(1\) or \(2\). If it is \(2\), coverage forces the first entry to be \(1\). If the last entry is \(1\), then the first entry is either \(1\) or \(2\): if it were at least \(3\), coverage would also require a \(2\), but the only two positions would already have values at least \(3\) and \(1\). Thus
\[
 b_2=3.
\]

Now define \(a(0)=1\), \(a(1)=3\), and
\[
 a(n+2)=2a(n+1)+2a(n).
\]
We prove by induction on \(n\) that
\[
 b_{n+1}=a(n). \tag{5}
\]
For \(n=0\) and \(n=1\), this is exactly \(b_1=1\) and \(b_2=3\). For \(n\ge0\), assuming the two preceding identities, the recurrence for the good tuples gives
\[
 b_{n+3}=2b_{n+2}+2b_{n+1}
       =2a(n+1)+2a(n)
       =a(n+2).
\]
Thus (5) holds for every \(n\ge0\). This proves the claimed interpretation: \(a(n)\) is the number of length-\(n+1\) sequences of positive integers which cover an initial interval and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing.

For completeness, this is the same sequence as the canonical ternary-word enumeration. Let \(c_n\) be the number of words of length \(n\) over \(\{0,1,2\}\) having no two consecutive zeros. There is one empty word, so \(c_0=1\), and all three one-letter words are allowed, so \(c_1=3\). For a valid word of length \(n+2\), either its last symbol is \(1\) or \(2\), giving two choices appended to any valid word of length \(n+1\), or its last symbol is \(0\). In the latter case its penultimate symbol must be \(1\) or \(2\), giving two choices appended, together with a final \(0\), to any valid prefix of length \(n\). These cases are disjoint and exhaustive, so
\[
 c_{n+2}=2c_{n+1}+2c_n.
\]
Since \((c_n)\) and \((a(n))\) have the same two initial values and the same recurrence, \(c_n=a(n)\) for every \(n\). Combining this with (5), both the ternary strings of length \(n\) avoiding consecutive zeros and the stated good sequences of length \(n+1\) are counted by \(a(n)\), as required.
